 I t looks like a typo, as if it’s someone’s twisted April Fool’s gag went public, or maybe a die-hard fan’s fantasy list posted in some obscure chatroom.
 It’s not.
 Lobos fans now live in a world where their football team is nationally ranked.
 Friday on TV
 What: New Mexico (7-1, 4-0 in MWC) at Nevada (3-5, 2-2), 7 p.m.
 Where: Mackay Stadium, Reno, Nev.
 TV: CBS Sports Network
 Radio: KKOB 96.3 FM
 Live stats: www.GoLobos.com/fbstats 
 For the first time in school history, the University of New Mexico football team finds itself in the Top 25. After surviving Saturday’s 21-16 nail-biter at San Jose State, the Lobos are 7-1 for just the second time in 88 years and now a part of the two major weekly tabulations that are updated every Sunday.
 The voters in The Associated Press media poll have UNM No. 22, while a panel of head coaches from around the country — which includes Lobos coach Jason Eck — have them at No. 25 in the USA Today /American Football Coaches Association poll.
 A spate of losses of teams ranked Nos. 19-25 last weekend opened the door for a little history. Five teams entering the weekend in the AP window — SMU, Northwestern, Arizona, Oklahoma State and Wisconsin — all lost.
 The Lobos have gained national fame this season with their stellar defensive play. They have allowed 20 points or fewer in 12 straight games, including all eight this season. It’s the longest such stretch for a non-power school since Louisiana Tech in 1992.
 The Lobos are now ranked in front of Arizona, South Carolina and Florida in the AP poll. Arizona’s coaching staff includes Danny Gonzales, UNM’s coach for four seasons between 2020 and 2023.
 New Mexico is one of only two non-power conference teams in the polls, joining Boise State. The Broncos survived their own scare Saturday night, using a late rally to beat Texas State after blowing a 25-point halftime lead.
 Boise State maintained its No. 20 ranking in the AP and rose one spot to No. 21 in the AFCA poll.
 Tuesday night brings us the initial College Football Playoff ranking that is used to determine the 12-team playoff field in December. The team ranked highest among the Group of 6 non-power conferences receives an automatic bid to the playoffs.
 Boise State is expected to be the top G6 team in the initial CFP ranking with New Mexico a close second. The Lobos lead the Mountain West standings with a 4-0 mark heading into Friday night’s game at Nevada, making it the first time they’ll ever play a game with a number next to their name.
 Asked after Saturday’s game what a ranking does for the program, Eck said it’s a reward for the fans but wasn’t sure what impact it will have on his team.
 “It doesn’t change a lot,” he said. “You know, we got a short week [to prepare for Nevada]. … It’s completely out of our control how people vote so we’re not too worried about that, how it looks.”
 UNM has been playing football since 1892 and only rarely been poll-worthy in the media’s eyes. The AP began publishing a Top 20 in 1934, reduced it to 10 teams for a few years in the 60s and expanded it from 20 to 25 teams in 1989.
 New Mexico’s 1982 team ended the season 10-1 and came close in the final regular-season AP and UPI rankings but never got in. The 1997 team started 6-0 and was 9-2 as WAC Mountain Division champion before losing in the WAC title game to Colorado State, then to Arizona in the Insight.com Bowl.
 UNM head coach Jason Eck walks the sidelines during a Sept. 26 game against New Mexico State in Aggie Memorial Stadium.
 Jim Weber/New Mexican file photo 
 Both seasons proved to be the last for the head coaches of those teams: Joe Morrison took the job at South Carolina after the ‘82 season and Dennis Franchione left for TCU prior to the 1998 campaign.
 New Mexico has actually made two appearances in the various iterations of the coaches’ poll, doing so in 1964 when it was No. 16 in the final ranking and again in 1997 when it was No. 25 — both appearances came in the last poll of the regular season.
 Expectations for this year’s Lobos have always been high. The team won nine games last season and returned more starters than any team in the Mountain West. Its only loss so far was Sept. 19 at then-No. 24 Oklahoma.
 The Lobos’ defense has been among the best in the country all season, ranking fourth in yards allowed (258.1) and first in points allowed (11.88), interceptions (17) and turnover margin (plus-17).
 “I think we have a historic defense,” Eck said when asked if the his team’s current formula of success — strong defense saving the day for a struggling offense — is sustainable over the final four games of the regular season.
 “When you’re playing with a historically good defense, yeah, I think it is,” he said. “Obviously that puts a lot of pressure [on the defense] if all of a sudden they have a game where they give, you know, 24 or we may be in trouble. So, we gotta get better with our passing game, no question, and i think that’s going to be a big point of emphasis.”
 ESPN’s weekly Power Index lists New Mexico at 46th. It measures a team’s strength based on a series of analytics. It gives the Lobos a 66.1% chance of winning the Mountain West and a 15.2% chance of making the CFP.
